title: Joker: Folie á Deux: A Tragedy and a Takedown

commenti.body:
I don't know why you're being down voted. This is such a succinct and specific post describing what you liked about the movie.

I agree with all the points you made. I'll just add this: I also liked this movie, not as much as the first one though. Both had good depth, and Joker 1 was also very entertaining. However, Folie á Deux is just such a sad sad tragedy. There's no way in hell they were seeking to satisfy the same demographic that 'enjoyed' the first one.

I dislike the argument that this didn't work because they were no longer following an amazing mold like the first one (i.e. king of comedy). That's just lazy. Yes, they did play with expectations. Was that wrong? I guess it depends who you ask. This is the problem with sequels: You have to make something different, but not so different. You have to make it similar, but not too similar.

Yes, and hitting that golden balance (if it objectively exists, that is) is a very daunting task.

I feel like Folie á Deux has gotten enough bad press there isn't much room for discussion left... sadly. Perhaps when it all cools down there'll be a better time. But I am glad you responded and engaged honestly.

At the very least I had an outlet to praise the movie. Which is something it deserves.

>  The musical numbers got better and better with each new insert, and I admire both the concept and the execution of it all being a set of interludes showcasing the highly internalized yet vibrant thoughts, fears and fantasies of Arthur and Harley.

Hard disagree.  The musical numbers are a farce.  If someone is a fan of musicals, there's pretty much no other musical that is as poorly and purposely *less* choreographed than the musicals in FoD.  Fleck is at home, watching old Astaire and Rogers pictures - especially *Shall We Dance*, their most celebrated.  When he goes into his imagination, he should be dancing like them.  

Phoenix and Gaga sing mostly out of tune and in a talky kind of way.  Gaga occasionally show that she can actually sing, but then is immediately restrained.  And we all know Phoenix *can* sing, from his work in *Walk the Line.*

I don't know where the $200M went for this movie, but it didn't go into it becoming a musical.  Those pieces of the movie were done on the cheap.  Contrast that with Spielberg's *West Side Story* - a soaring, extravagant musical, which costs *half* of *Folie a Deux*, at $100M. 

> But the story itself is also a major asset in the equation.

Very hard disagree.  The film’s entire premise—its dramatic spine—is nonsensical. Arthur Fleck is imprisoned in the abusive Arkham Asylum, awaiting trial. His defense attorney, Maryanne Stuart (Keener), mounts an insanity defense to ensure he receives the mental health treatment he desperately needs… in Arkham Asylum? And to secure this conviction, she instructs Fleck to behave as sensibly and normal as possible? Nothing about this plot makes sense. Fleck fires Stuart halfway through the trial—as if this were a dramatic turning point—but the action has no clear direction. What’s gained? What’s lost? The film offers no consistent thread of drama to follow.

>  So he acquiesces, drops his defense and admits to everything whilst denying the existence of the Joker.

In a better written movie, this might be defensible.  2019's *Joker* is a great script and 2024's *Folie a Deux* is inexcusably self-contradictory.  *Folie à Deux* reads more like an apology, or a reactionary response to the politically charged attacks of bigotry leveled at 2019’s *Joker*. One wonders if Phillips and Phoenix, despite the billion-dollar success of the original, were swayed by these baseless criticisms and compelled to accept the scornful labels of racism and misogyny. Do they really believe it’s necessary for Arthur Fleck, in full Joker regalia, to address the audience, camera, and jury to clarify that he’s the bad guy? As if we were unsure? Apparently so—because, without a shred of irony, he does.

\>If someone is a fan of musicals, there's pretty much no other musical that is as poorly and purposely *less* choreographed than the musicals in FoD

Ah, well, I'm not one, which would explain much. But even if I was, there's no guaranteed I'd hate.

\>And we all know Phoenix *can* sing, from his work in *Walk the Line.*

Not sure if this is an entirely fair comparison. You're talking about Phoenix 19 years younger than he was during shooting Joker 2.

\>to ensure he receives the mental health treatment he desperately needs… in Arkham Asylum?

Can't quite recall if it was Arkham Asylum she wanted to lead Arthur's therapy, but even if it was, it'd make  sense with the shittiness of the world portrayed - the only institution around to provide any form of counseling is an objectively fucked one. I do remember, however, that Stewart's priority was saving Arthur's life, preventing him from dying on an electric chair.

\>And to secure this conviction, she instructs Fleck to behave as sensibly and normal as possible?

Yup. First, the court needed to see Arthur. Remember, we only saw the first two trial days with Stewart leading the defense. We don't know what the rest of her plan was. My best guess is she'd order Arthur to have the Joker come out at some point, but in a "controlled" manner, so that the insanity plea/split personality defense would flow well. But, alas we didn't see that because Arthur went full Joker and sacked her willingly.

\>What’s gained? What’s lost?

I'll tell you how I see it. Arthur gains the control of his side of story, which was led by Stewart up to that point. And what he loses is a chance for a credible defense that could've saved his life. Now, of course Arthur doesn't care about that, but Stewart, some of his fans (especially given the uproar at the verdict later on, and that's AFTER he ditched the Joker) and the audiences do.

And also, this is a clear set up for the scene with Gary Puddles. It doesn't work the way it does unless Arthur gets to engage with him as a witness, and in the way Joker would. The scene would be drastically different if with Stewart in the equation.

\>Do they really believe it’s necessary for Arthur Fleck, in full Joker regalia, to address the audience, camera, and jury to clarify that he’s the bad guy? As if we were unsure? Apparently so—because, without a shred of irony, he does.

It's a conflicting matter. Personally, I don't see anything wrong with it. For the moment is not meant to function solely on a meta level (which it does work on, because believe me, the reception to the first movie went beyond the most likely intended reaction - it seemed the main talking point after the release was the gleeful, bloody terror of Arthur's rage and how "freeing" and relatable it felt to people... not the poignant, grim suffering he experienced before. I was in the discourse, I saw how little sympathy anyone had for Murrary, Randall or the Waynes), but first and foremost - on a narrative one. Arthur rejecting the Joker as a way of being and as his icon status was meant to trigger the reaction of his "fandom". Naturally, the fallout isn't uniform or super immediate (as we see fans escorting Arthur away post-explosion), but the myth fades quickly, the first sign of it being a huge chunk of trial spectators and Harley leaving the courthouse fresh after Fleck's confession. It underscores the trivality and shallowness of celebrity culture/fandom. As soon as Arthur speaks honestly, from his heart, with none of the theatricality and over-the-top hatred, he is rejected and declared a sellout. Later on Harley straight up tells him she only cared for him because of "the Joker".

> But even if I was, there's no guaranteed I'd hate

But it does speak to the intentions of Phillips and Phoenix.  *They* must be familiar good musicals, especially because they so prominently feature *Shall We Dance* in both movies.  They are purposely making a *bad* musical...and that should inform how the film should be analyzed.

> You're talking about Phoenix 19 years younger than he was during shooting Joker 2.

In a movie, you can sing and sing until you get the right take.  They are purposely using takes in which he is singly poorly, and they are purposely underutilizing Gaga as a singer and performer.  Combined with the poor and lackluster choreography and musical numbers, they are clearly and intentionally making a movie that a fan of musicals would dislike.  This is intentional subversion.

>  Can't quite recall if it was Arkham Asylum she wanted to lead Arthur's therapy, but even if it was, it'd make sense with the shittiness of the world portrayed - the only institution around to provide any form of counseling is an objectively fucked one.

This is all cope.  If he was in a regular jail, fighting his case with an insanity defense to get into Arkham would make sense.  That he's already there is careless writing.

>  My best guess is she'd order Arthur to have the Joker come out at some point, but in a "controlled" manner, so that the insanity plea/split personality defense would flow well.

You are adding intentions and motivations into the story that aren't there.  If Stuart was "playing" Arthur, seeding his eventual turn to the Joker to demonstrate his Jekyll and Hyde persona - that was clearly not in the screenplay.  If it was, we might think the story was clever.  But it's not, and you're making a defense of it as if it were there.

>  Arthur gains the control of his side of story, which was led by Stewart up to that point. And what he loses is a chance for a credible defense that could've saved his life.

Make this make sense.  What line of questioning is Stuart engaged in that is so categorically off the rails that Fleck needs to step in and change course?  How does he change course from what Stuart was pursuing?  How is he saving his life by *fully* embracing his Joker persona - if only by some convoluted twisting of luck and reason - when the only way an insanity defense would work...is if he fully embraces his Joker persona (???)  None of this makes any sense.

>  And also, this is a clear set up for the scene with Gary Puddles. It doesn't work the way it does unless Arthur gets to engage with him as a witness, and in the way Joker would. The scene would be drastically different if with Stewart in the equation.

Drastically different?  Aside from the admittedly hilarious Foghorn Leghorn routine, what would be different?  Seriously.  I mean, what defensive strategy would she invoke that was so polar opposite from what Fleck did, and *how* would that strategy have better served him?  Because, as far as I can tell, the logic should be that the more Joker he goes - the more likely his insanity defense would pan out...but Stuart is actively and purposely shielding the Joker persona as much as possible.

>  It underscores the trivality and shallowness of celebrity culture/fandom. As soon as Arthur speaks honestly, from his heart, with none of the theatricality and over-the-top hatred, he is rejected and declared a sellout. Later on Harley straight up tells him she only cared for him because of "the Joker".

There's very little subtext in the film about celebrity status, in the strictest sense of the word.  There is subtext about our bizarre fascination with criminals.  Harley is a paraphiliac - a woman attracted to killers, which is a rare, but not entirely uncommon phenomenon.  But this film isn't interested even in exploring that.  And, due to how purposely hostile the film is as a musical, a sequel, as a comic book movie, and as a film in a franchise - the subtext is more of a *response* to the charges of misogyny and racism the first movie unfairly endured.  

Phillips and Phoenix really took that criticism seriously enough to make a cinematic response, with having Joker admit to the camera/audience that he's the villian...before he is unceremoniously dispatched with to avoid any future films.

\>Combined with the poor and lackluster choreography and musical numbers, they are clearly and intentionally making a movie that a fan of musicals would dislike. This is intentional subversion.

Well, I'm sorry you didn't like this, but I can't really respond with anything but "I did, though". I'd also like to point out it's almost all unreal - a delusion playing out in Arthur's mind.

\>This is all cope. If he was in a regular jail, fighting his case with an insanity defense to get into Arkham would make sense. That he's already there is careless writing.

Urgh. Once again, this is one detail I'm fuzzy about because I do not remember if Stewart wanted Arkham specifically as the counseling facility. But the choice to put him there is not careless because it speaks to the incompetence and cruelty of the state - instead of properly assessing Arthur psychologically and/or putting him in solitary confinement, they throw him into a nuthouse because he acts like a loony.

\>What line of questioning is Stuart engaged in that is so categorically off the rails that Fleck needs to step in and change course? How does he change course from what Stuart was pursuing? How is he saving his life by *fully* embracing his Joker persona - if only by some convoluted twisting of luck and reason - when the only way an insanity defense would work...is if he fully embraces his Joker persona (???) None of this makes any sense.

This is behind the point. Arthur is not there to walk away alive. Both these movies he's borderline suicidal at worst and divorced from the want to live at best. One of his delusions has him blow his brains out, for crying out loud. The only reason Arthur fires Stewart is because Harley influences him. She makes him believe taking over the trial at least in part as the Joker will allow him to take some control of his own life - as well as see the "love" the masses of Gotham have for him. And it sort of works - Arthur gets a platform and his "fans" respond - both in the courtroom and in prison, with what the "Oh When The Saints" mini riot scene. You're assuming the firing of Stewart was supposed to be "logical", when it was not. It made sense for the character, but it wasn't common sense.

\>Drastically different? Aside from the admittedly hilarious Foghorn Leghorn routine, what would be different? Seriously. I mean, what defensive strategy would she invoke that was so polar opposite from what Fleck did, and *how* would that strategy have better served him? Because, as far as I can tell, the logic should be that the more Joker he goes - the more likely his insanity defense would pan out...but Stuart is actively and purposely shielding the Joker persona as much as possible.

On a narrative level, it would not work as well. Arthur needs to engage Gary directly, being in control of his "side of the story", as the supposed "defense" of himself. And he has to do when being arrogant and confident. If Arthur is to reject the Joker, as per the story's intent, he has to be shown its failings headfirst. A meek, slightly withdrawn Arthur wouldn't see it as clearly.

\>Harley is a paraphiliac - a woman attracted to killers, which is a rare, but not entirely uncommon phenomenon. But this film isn't interested even in exploring that. And, due to how purposely hostile the film is as a musical, a sequel, as a comic book movie, and as a film in a franchise - the subtext is more of a *response* to the charges of misogyny and racism the first movie unfairly endured.

I honestly struggle to make sense of this tangent. How in the hell can you suggest the movie isn't interested in exploring all this? Arthur's renewed descent into the Joker hinges on Harley believing in the fantasy zealously, even moreso than the man himself does. All of their scenes together show Harley being interested in the Joker only. When they fuck, it has to be with Arthur wearing his make-up. In the courthouse, Harley is mad at Stewart for trying to suppress what she believes is Arthur's true self. Finally, Harley dons the makeup herself and quite literally becomes the female Joker. And have we forgotten that Arthur's icon status finds fertile ground even in the strict, controlled Arkham, when he incites a mini riot with "Oh When The Saints"? And it's that icon status that leads to the death of his quasi-friend Ricky. And when it's destroyed, so is Arthur. For he is killed by his most zealous of fans, one that lurked in the background quietly, but absorbed the myth with insane enthusiasm. And so the zealot kills the false idol for betraying the myth.

> But the choice to put him there is not careless because it speaks to the incompetence and cruelty of the state - instead of properly assessing Arthur psychologically and/or putting him in solitary confinement, they throw him into a nuthouse because he acts like a loony.

Would you at least grant that it would make more sense if Fleck was locked up with hardened criminals throughout his trial, and his defense attorney wanted to get him into a psychiatric ward instead?  

> The only reason Arthur fires Stewart is because Harley influences him. She makes him believe taking over the trial at least in part as the Joker will allow him to take some control of his own life - as well as see the "love" the masses of Gotham have for him.

Okay, but think about it.  What line of questioning is Stuart engaged in that would elicit such a response from Fleck?  Does he "take over" and then change course with the questioning?  Other than donning the Joker persona, does he engage with any line of questioning that Stuart wouldn't?

What I'm getting at is that if the motivation for Fleck is to "release the Joker", then there should have been a catalyzing moment that *made sense* for him to do so.  Moreover, it was the first time in the entire movie that his character has any agency.  So, it's all the more important for his character to meaningfully take over the story.  If Stuart had been egging Fleck on in order to force an emotional outburst - that could be interesting.  If Stuart discussed what their strategy was with Puddles and Fleck took over because he didn't agree with it, that could be interesting.  If Fleck was lost in his mind...singing and dancing and inadvertently comes to - firing his attorney almost against his own cognizance, and then is forced to play along...*that* could be interesting.

But instead, Stuart is engaged in a completely banal line of questioning with Puddles, and Fleck inexplicably protests - but there's no *reason* that makes any sense.

If you're okay with it...then you're having to add something to the story - underlying motivations or whatever - in order to justify that it *worked* for you.  But objectively, it's bonehead writing.

>  If Arthur is to reject the Joker, as per the story's intent, he has to be shown its failings headfirst.

If point of the movie was for Arthur to reject the Joker, the movie would have been different from the first scene onwards.  How do poorly executed musical numbers lead to Arthur rejecting the Joker persona?  Why even build a movie around the courtroom drama genre if the point is for Arthur to reject Joker?  I mean, you could have a movie that starts with a prison break and Fleck/Joker escape and during his run as an outlaw, he decides it's too much and rejects Joker.  So, why the courtroom drama?  Why didn't Fleck reject the Joker persona infront of Harley - which makes the most sense thematically?  Why, instead, does he do so to the jury/camera/audience?

I think the point of the courtroom drama is to put the audience in the jury box and Joker - as a stand in for the 2019 film - on trial.  And for Phillips and Phoenix, as a mea culpa, confess that they were wrong in glorifying all of the violence and what not in the first film.

>Would you at least grant that it would make more sense if Fleck was locked up with hardened criminals throughout his trial, and his defense attorney wanted to get him into a psychiatric ward instead?

Technically... if the system hadn't been established to be as shit as it is. But it was, so almost any cruelty is informed and explained by default. And remember, Stewart's primary goal is to save Arthur's life.

>What I'm getting at is that if the motivation for Fleck is to "release the Joker", then there should have been a catalyzing moment that made sense for him to do so. Moreover, it was the first time in the entire movie that his character has any agency.

I already explained why he chose to do that. Harley convinced him to do it to splash some of his style onto the trial and therefore incite his fans. If he turned the trial on its head as the Joker, the "fandom" would respond and he'd see he is indeed "loved" in a way. Also, given Harley was on somewhat shakey ground after Arthur confronted her about her lies, this was her way of making herself appear more genuine: "See, if you do this, you'll see it's not just me who's rooting for you. There are more like you than you think".

>If you're okay with it...then you're having to add something to the story - underlying motivations or whatever - in order to justify that it worked for you. But objectively, it's bonehead writing.

I am NOT adding anything. Harley wanting Arthur to be the Joker all the time is there from the start. Arthur wanting admiration and love is there from the start. He embraces the shadow-clown once again for the woman he thinks is there for him and people he thinks there are for him. It is not about Stewart specifically or any strategy of hers. And I don't deal in "objective" terms.

>How do poorly executed musical numbers lead to Arthur rejecting the Joker persona?

They're something different. They're a representation of his delusions, plans, fantasies. Look at the "There's Always a Joker" number: through the lyrics, Arthur explains who he is in the eyes of the state and society and how he didn't know what to do about it until he became aware of it: "The fate deals the hand and I see... The Joker is ME!"... But that's just the vocals. Everything else - Arthur disrupting the courtroom procedure, killing Prosecutor Dent and Judge Rothwax, THEN himself - is a representation of what he wants to do with all those that marginalize, ridicule and harm, and then end himself. That's what his fantasy is. In other numbers, Arthur plans his future life with Harley, but is also having moments of doubt - hence his daydream where Harley sucker-shoots him in the abdomen (which returns in his actual death).

>I think the point of the courtroom drama is to put the audience in the jury box and Joker - as a stand in for the 2019 film - on trial. And for Phillips and Phoenix, as a mea culpa, confess that they were wrong in glorifying all of the violence and what not in the first film.

You've got the meta right, I'll give you that. But you're not looking at the narrative in isolation. Hear me out. Why all of this was done? It's because it's not just Harley who believed in the myth of the Joker. It's all those clown-masked people, the rioters, the looters, the fans with transparent, inmates like Ricky and the zealot - quite a sizeable chunk of Gotham's population. They needed to hear it from Arthur, too. And then abandon him for it, like the shallow bitches they were. They couldn't accept that deep down Arthur never wanted to burn everything down and revel in the wanton destruction. All he wanted was to make people laugh with his jokes. I must mention here another reason he retreats into the Joker: a fundamental tenet of his existence was shattered. He learned that his mother was never on board with him being a comedian and only thought he'd fit right in because he could laugh at his own jokes with "that dumb laugh". As if being an abusive mother wasn't bad enough, Penny also made fun of her son's own condition. But the retreat into the Joker did not work either. Not only did Gary suffer emotional damage because of Arthur's crimes, not only was Arthur unable to use the Joker against the violation he suffered from the Arkham guards, but one of his fans, Ricky, was killed because he spread his message too much, singing "Oh When The Saints" until the guards ended him. So Arthur gave up on all of it. He could never become a comedian, but being the Joker was also useless against an all-powerful state that was able to break him even harder despite everything he did to appear above it. And so Fleck cut the clown off entirely. But that's when he lost the last shreds of any connection to the outside world. Most of his fans walked out on him. And the ones that didn't appeared to him like deranged sycophants. Why do you think he sprang out of the car impromptu and ran like his life depended on it from the people that were there to "save" him? Because they talked of actually destroying the city of Gotham. Arthur was done with the senseless violence. And about everything else.

> And remember, Stewart's primary goal is to save Arthur's life.

And to get him psychiatric care...which Batman lore would place in Arkham Asylum...which he is already in.

>   Harley convinced him to do it to splash some of his style onto the trial and therefore incite his fans.

I don't mind that Fleck "explodes" in the Courtroom and begins his public transformation into Joker.  I mind that what catalyzed him to do so - and the entire legal strategy that it impacted - made no sense.  Just because Harley wants him to go full Joker, doesn't mean it makes sense for him to do so in the middle of the line of questioning with Puddles.  When he comes into the courtroom as Joker, he has no plan to meaningfully engage with Puddles that would point back as to his frame of mind as to why he had his outburst to fire Stuart.  Are we to think that Fleck's exasperation at Stuart's line of questioning is because she's not challenging Puddles' legal name?  I don't think so.

>   They're a representation of his delusions...But that's just the vocals. Everything else - Arthur disrupting the courtroom procedure, killing Prosecutor Dent and Judge Rothwax, THEN himself - is a representation of what he wants to do with all those that marginalize, ridicule and harm, and then end himself.

I don't dispute that.  I'm talking about the execution of the musical numbers themselves.  If they are fantasy, that's all the more reason to go balls out and make a big production out of it.  That's all the more reason for him to sing like he knows how to sing, and dance and entertain well beyond what his "real life" character is capable of doing.  Phillips and Phoenix are purposely making something *less* entertaining than it can be, and hoping the irony of saying, "That's entertainment," somehow lets them off the hook artistically.

>  He learned that his mother was never on board with him being a comedian and only thought he'd fit right in because he could laugh at his own jokes with "that dumb laugh". As if being an abusive mother wasn't bad enough, Penny also made fun of her son's own condition. 

I found this bout of exposition another example of piss-poor writing.  It's so baffling to me because the script for 2019's Joker is extremely well polished.  But, the script for Folie a Duex is just overloaded with problems.

Considering how grounded the 2019's Joker was, does it make any sense that the neighbor Sophie went to Fleck's apartment and his mother just spilled everything to her about Fleck like she testifies to?  If she's saying this to a neighbor down the hall on their first visit, she would be telling strangers about Fleck his whole life.  It's just uncharacteristic that she would be saying these things to other people and the first time Fleck hears about it is in this situation.

I understand that the script wants to further isolate Fleck from his mother - but he's already killed her.  This is unnecessary and breaks the internal consistency of the world that has been built.

> They couldn't accept that deep down Arthur never wanted to burn everything down and revel in the wanton destruction. All he wanted was to make people laugh with his jokes...Arthur was done with the senseless violence. And about everything else.

I get it, but the script doesn't create a consistent line of drama, nor is it presented in a quality fashion, to sell this point convincingly.  It's in the text, clouded by distractions, and nothing more.

>I mind that what catalyzed him to do so - and the entire legal strategy that it impacted - made no sense. Just because Harley wants him to go full Joker, doesn't mean it makes sense for him to do so in the middle of the line of questioning with Puddles.

I repeat - there is no strategy when it comes to the Joker. Arthur randomly fires his attorney and kisses her while at it because it's the kind of chaotic, social-more-defying behavior that's expected of the Joker. He's leaning into the act, hoping it'll make him feel more in control, powerful, and seen. There is no strategy when it comes to dealing with Gary except... seeing if he too likes the new Arthur. And to Fleck's dismay, he does not. Not at all.

>Phillips and Phoenix are purposely making something less entertaining than it can be

Alas, it was entertaining enough for me.

>If she's saying this to a neighbor down the hall on their first visit, she would be telling strangers about Fleck his whole life. It's just uncharacteristic that she would be saying these things to other people and the first time Fleck hears about it is in this situation.

It becomes more believable once you take into account that A. Arthur has been invisible almost his entire life, not knowing who he truly was to add insult to injury. That, and he'd been cut off from the outside world behind the cold walls of Arkham, and B. Penny at the time was an elderly and ill person, and she acted very meekly the whole first movie. Is her being more open about the past this unbelievable? Also, we can assume Sophie presented herself as someone close to Arthur who wanted to learn something about him.


>I understand that the script wants to further isolate Fleck from his mother - but he's already killed her. This is unnecessary and breaks the internal consistency of the world that has been built.

It doesn't. What it actually does is remove one of the few frail foundations of Arthur's existence. For as long as he lived he believed comedy and making others laugh was his purpose. So what happens when that foundation was something his mother just told him to do because she thought he had a dumb laugh - which was actually his condition?

>I get it, but the script doesn't create a consistent line of drama, nor is it presented in a quality fashion, to sell this point convincingly. It's in the text, clouded by distractions, and nothing more.

I guess I won't be able to convince you...

>  So what happens when that foundation was something his mother just told him to do because she thought he had a dumb laugh - which was actually his condition?

You're conveniently forgetting that in 2019's Joker, Fleck's ambition to become a comedian is already untethered to his mother's wishes.  She has already voiced her doubts and apprehension about him being a comic saying, "Don't you have to be funny?"  His mother is already established as *not* wanting him to pursue a career in comedy.  You're forgetting this just like the screenwriter for *Folie a Deux* forgot this.

These two things are not the same. It's one thing to voice your doubts about something you've formerly encouraged a family member to do, but it's another to gaslight them into making it their future while making fun of their condition behind their back.

And no, I have not conveniently forgotten anything, it's simply been a while since I watched Joker.
